name: Czech Republic
tagline: Prague's fairy-tale skyline, fairy-tale towns beyond it, and a beer culture so central to daily life that pubs function as the country's real town squares.
cardDescription: Prague Castle and Charles Bridge, the fairy-tale town of Český Krumlov, spa colonnades in Karlovy Vary, and Moravian wine country beyond.
metaDescription: A complete Czech Republic travel guide: the 10 best places to visit, trains, food, costs, etiquette and a nine-day itinerary.

image.file: File:Czech-03993 - Boat Station & St. Vitus Cathedral (32980108646).jpg
image.alt: Prague's skyline along the Vltava River, with St Vitus Cathedral rising above Prague Castle

intro: The Czech Republic is genuinely one of Central Europe's most rewarding destinations, its capital Prague among the continent's most beautiful and best-preserved historic cities, its hundred spires largely untouched by the wars that levelled so much of the region.

Beyond Prague, the country genuinely rewards slower exploration — fairy-tale towns like Český Krumlov, spa resorts like Karlovy Vary, and a Moravian region in the east with its own wine culture, dialect and noticeably slower pace.
It's also genuinely a country built for beer, home to the world's first pale lager and a pub culture that runs through daily life as a genuine social institution rather than sitting apart from it.
placesIntro: Ordered roughly by how strongly we would recommend each for a first visit — though Moravia rewards a second trip just as much as a first.
thingsToDoIntro: The experiences that recur across the country and make a Czech Republic trip feel like more than a checklist of castles.

thingsToDo.title: Drink a proper Czech pilsner

image.alt: A glass of Czech pilsner beer

thingsToDo.text: A genuinely essential Czech experience, in the country that invented pale lager and still drinks more beer per capita than anywhere else on Earth.
thingsToDo.tip: Genuinely order by the round in a proper pub — a server will keep bringing beers until you place a coaster over your glass.

thingsToDo.title: Watch the Prague Astronomical Clock strike the hour

image.file: File:The Prague Astronomical Clock in Old Town - 8559.jpg
image.alt: The Prague Astronomical Clock in Old Town Square

thingsToDo.text: A genuinely medieval spectacle, the clock's procession of apostle figures still drawing a crowd every hour, just as it has since 1410.
thingsToDo.tip: Genuinely the view is better than the show itself — watch from a café terrace rather than fighting the crowd below.

thingsToDo.title: Soak up a thermal spa town's colonnades

image.alt: The Mill Colonnade in the spa town of Karlovy Vary

thingsToDo.text: A genuinely elegant tradition, sipping mineral spring water from a spa cup while strolling ornate 19th-century colonnades.
thingsToDo.tip: Genuinely buy a lázeňský oplatek (spa wafer) from a colonnade kiosk to go with the mineral water.

thingsToDo.title: Wander a fairy-tale old town away from Prague's crowds

image.file: File:Old town in Český Krumlov with Jelení lávka, 20250504 1251 8862.jpg
image.alt: The old town of Český Krumlov beside the Vltava River

thingsToDo.text: A genuinely different pace from the capital, Bohemia's smaller UNESCO towns offering the same architecture with a fraction of the visitors.
thingsToDo.tip: Genuinely stay overnight if you can — day-trippers clear out by early evening, leaving these towns wonderfully quiet.

thingsToDo.title: Taste Moravian wine straight from a village cellar

image.file: File:Blatnice pod Svatým Antonínkem, wine cellars 01.jpg
image.alt: Traditional wine cellars in a Moravian village

thingsToDo.text: A genuinely different side of Czech drinking culture, South Moravia's rolling vineyards producing wine most visitors never expect to find here.
thingsToDo.tip: Genuinely rent a bicycle to tour several village cellars along the region's marked wine trails.

thingsToDo.title: Explore a country castle or chateau garden
thingsToDo.text: A genuinely rewarding day out, the Czech countryside scattered with more castles and chateaux per square kilometre than almost anywhere in Europe.
thingsToDo.tip: Genuinely book interior tours ahead in summer — the most famous chateaux sell out their guided time slots.

foodIntro: Czech food genuinely means hearty, warming classics built around meat, dumplings and, of course, beer.

foods.name: Svíčková (marinated beef in cream sauce)

image.alt: Svíčková, marinated beef in cream sauce with bread dumplings

foods.text: Genuinely the national dish for many Czechs, tender beef in a vegetable cream sauce, served with bread dumplings and a dollop of cranberry sauce.

foods.name: Guláš with dumplings

image.alt: Czech goulash served with bread dumplings

foods.text: Genuinely a Czech take on goulash, a rich, paprika-spiced beef stew mopped up with sliced bread dumplings.

foods.name: Trdelník (chimney cake)

image.alt: Trdelník, a rolled pastry cooked over an open flame

foods.text: Genuinely more a Prague tourist-street tradition than an old Czech recipe, a sugar-and-cinnamon pastry cooked on a rotating spit.
foods.whereToTry: Street stalls throughout central Prague's tourist areas.

foods.name: Czech beer (pivo)

image.alt: A glass of classic Czech pale lager

foods.text: Genuinely the country's defining drink, from world-famous Pilsner Urquell to countless excellent small regional breweries.
foods.whereToTry: Pubs and breweries in every town, large and small.

foods.name: Smažený sýr (fried cheese)

image.file: File:Smažený sýr s tatarskou omáčkou a brambory.jpg
image.alt: Smažený sýr, breaded fried cheese with tartar sauce and potatoes

foods.text: Genuinely a beloved pub classic, breaded and deep-fried cheese served with tartar sauce and fries or potatoes.

foods.name: Koláče (fruit-filled pastries)

image.alt: Traditional koláče pastries filled with fruit

foods.text: Genuinely a homely regional favourite, soft yeasted pastry rounds topped with fruit, poppyseed or sweet cheese.
foods.whereToTry: Bakeries and cafés throughout Bohemia and Moravia.

practicalIntro: The essentials for planning a Czech Republic trip, gathered in one place.

practical.language: Czech, a West Slavic language; English is widely understood in Prague and other tourist areas, less so in smaller towns.
practical.money: Genuinely widely card-friendly in cities and larger towns, though cash still helps at small pubs, markets and rural guesthouses.
practical.visa: Schengen Area member; visa-free entry for up to 90 days in any 180-day period for many nationalities including the US, Canada, Australia and the UK.
practical.plugs: Type C and E, 230 V, 50 Hz.
practical.emergency: 112 for general emergencies nationwide; 158 police, 155 ambulance, 150 fire.
practical.tipping: Not obligatory but genuinely expected — around 10% at restaurants, told to the server rather than left on the table.
practical.safety: Genuinely one of Europe's safer countries, with petty theft and currency-exchange scams around busy Prague tourist spots the main things to watch for.
practical.connectivity: Genuinely excellent 4G and 5G coverage, with wifi widely available in cafés and accommodation.
practical.timeZone: Central European Time (UTC+1), Central European Summer Time (UTC+2) from late March to late October.

budget.label: Backpacker
budget.value: Kč1,200–2,000 per day — hostels, tram tickets, pub lunches

budget.label: Mid-range
budget.value: Kč2,500–4,500 per day — 3-star hotels, restaurant dinners, museum entry

budget.label: Comfortable
budget.value: Kč5,500–9,000+ per day — boutique hotels, fine dining, private guides

budget.label: Day trip from Prague
budget.value: Add roughly Kč600–1,200 for transport and entry fees to Český Krumlov or Kutná Hora

bestTime.headline: May, June and September for the best balance of weather and crowds
bestTime.summary: The Czech Republic genuinely has warm, long days in summer and a magical Christmas market season, with the shoulder months offering the best overall value.

seasons.text: Genuinely mild temperatures, blooming parks and manageable crowds before peak summer arrives.
Genuinely the warmest, busiest season, with long evenings perfect for riverside terraces, though central Prague gets genuinely crowded.
Genuinely golden light over the castles and vineyards, with noticeably thinner crowds than summer.
Genuinely magical around Christmas markets and snow-dusted spires, though short days and cold call for proper layers.

bestTime.avoid: Genuinely nothing strongly, though August's heat and crowds in central Prague are worth planning around.

tripDuration.headline: 7–10 days for a first trip
tripDuration.summary: Genuinely a compact country, with Prague working as an easy hub for day trips before heading further afield.

options.text: Prague alone, at an unhurried pace.
options.detail: Genuinely enough for the castle, Old Town and a couple of nearby day trips.

options.text: Prague plus Český Krumlov and Kutná Hora.
options.detail: Genuinely a well-rounded first trip covering Bohemia's essentials.

options.text: The itinerary on this page: Prague, Kutná Hora, Český Krumlov, Karlovy Vary and Moravia.
options.detail: Genuinely a complete first look at both Bohemia and Moravia.

options.text: Add Plzeň, Bohemian Switzerland and slower travel through the Moravian wine country.
options.detail: Genuinely rewards travellers who want to go well beyond the highlights.

transport.intro: Genuinely one of Europe's best rail networks for a country this size, with buses filling in the gaps.

options.text: Genuinely the backbone of Czech travel between [[prague|Prague]], [[brno|Brno]], [[olomouc|Olomouc]] and [[plzen|Plzeň]].
options.detail: Frequent, comfortable and inexpensive compared to Western Europe.

options.text: Genuinely a comfortable, budget-friendly alternative on popular routes.
options.detail: Often cheaper than the train, with onboard snacks and entertainment on RegioJet.

options.text: Genuinely the easiest way to reach [[cesky-krumlov|Český Krumlov]] or [[kutna-hora|Kutná Hora]] without a car.
options.detail: Widely available and reasonably priced, though a direct train or bus is often just as easy.

options.text: Genuinely useful for [[bohemian-switzerland|Bohemian Switzerland]] and [[lednice-valtice|Lednice-Valtice]]'s wine country.
options.detail: Public transport reaches both, but a car gives far more flexibility.

options.detail: The easiest way to get around the capital itself.

itinerary.title: Nine days in Czech Republic

days.afternoon: Old Town Square and the Astronomical Clock.
days.evening: Dinner near Charles Bridge, lit up after dark.

days.morning: Prague Castle and St Vitus Cathedral.
days.afternoon: Malá Strana's lanes and palace gardens.
days.evening: Dinner at a restaurant with a castle view.

culture.intro: Czech culture genuinely blends a deep literary and musical tradition with a famously dry, understated sense of humour and one of the world's great beer cultures.

etiquette.title: Greetings are genuinely polite but reserved
etiquette.text: A firm handshake and direct eye contact are standard; save hugs for people you know well.

etiquette.title: Beer culture runs genuinely deep
etiquette.text: Ordering by the round and saying 'na zdraví' (cheers) before drinking is expected pub etiquette.

etiquette.title: Punctuality is genuinely valued
etiquette.text: Arrive on time for both social plans and reserved restaurant tables.

etiquette.title: Dress is genuinely practical and modest
etiquette.text: Smart-casual works almost everywhere; only the fanciest restaurants expect more.

etiquette.title: Small talk is genuinely kept brief
etiquette.text: Czechs tend to be direct and reserved with strangers, warming up considerably once you know them.

etiquette.title: Tipping is genuinely modest but expected
etiquette.text: Round up or add about 10% in restaurants, telling the server the total rather than leaving cash on the table.

dos: Say 'dobrý den' (good day) when entering small shops, cafés and pubs.
Validate public transport tickets before boarding — inspectors do check, and fines are steep.
Try a proper neighbourhood pub over a touristy one near major squares for better beer and prices.
Book Prague Castle's interiors and popular restaurants ahead in peak summer months.
donts: Don't expect tap water automatically at restaurants — ask, or you may be served, and charged for, bottled.
Don't jaywalk carelessly — Czech drivers expect pedestrians to use marked crossings.
Don't block a tram or metro doorway — step fully inside to let others board.
Don't rush Prague's Old Town at the expense of Bohemia and Moravia beyond it.

tipsIntro: Practical notes that make travel through the Czech Republic noticeably smoother.
tips: Buy genuinely a Prague public transport ticket or pass rather than risk an unvalidated-ticket fine.
Carry genuinely some cash for small pubs, markets and rural areas, even though cards are widely accepted.
Book genuinely Prague Castle's interiors and popular restaurants ahead in summer.
Learn genuinely a few basic Czech phrases — English is widely spoken in Prague but less so in smaller towns.
Pack genuinely comfortable shoes — most historic centres are best explored on foot over cobblestones.
Avoid genuinely currency exchange booths advertising 'no commission' — compare rates before handing over cash.
Try genuinely a lunch menu (denní menu) for the best-value midday meals at sit-down restaurants.
Consider genuinely basing yourself in Brno for a few days to explore Moravia at an easier pace.

faq.q: How many days do you need in the Czech Republic?
faq.a: Seven to ten days genuinely covers Prague plus day trips and a stretch of Moravia; three to four days suits a Prague-only visit.

faq.q: Is the Czech Republic on the euro?
faq.a: No, genuinely not — it uses the Czech koruna (Kč), even though it's an EU member.
Genuinely more affordable than Western Europe overall, though central Prague's restaurants and attractions have crept close to Western prices in recent years.

faq.q: Do you need a car to see the Czech Republic?
faq.a: No, genuinely not — trains and buses cover the country well, though a car helps for Bohemian Switzerland and the Moravian wine country.

faq.q: What's the difference between Bohemia and Moravia?
faq.a: Genuinely the country's two historic regions — Bohemia in the west around Prague, Moravia in the east around Brno, with its own dialect, wine and traditions.
Yes, genuinely — one of Europe's safer countries, with petty theft in busy Prague tourist spots the main thing to watch for.
